conclusion: C/C is the reference genotype at SIRT6 rs117385980 (GRCh38 chr19:4180588 C>T), carried by roughly 93-99% of people depending on ancestry (gnomAD v4 genomes T allele frequency 0.5-3.5%). In the Birjand Longitudinal Aging Study (Iran; 227 adults aged 60-90), every frail participant and every participant aged 80-90 had C/C, but none of these differences reached statistical significance. This genotype says nothing about an individual's lifespan or frailty risk.

C/T carries one T allele at SIRT6 rs117385980, an intronic variant (Ensembl, ClinGen: NM_016539.4:c.194+194G>A), not the stop-gain the source paper describes. Two small candidate-gene studies point the same way, and neither is statistically significant. In Finnish men, T carriers were more frequent among men who died of natural causes at about 67 than among long-lived healthy men (Fisher P=0.07; OR 3.53, 95% CI 0.96-13.4). In Iranian adults aged 60-90, T was absent at ages 80-90 (0/80 alleles vs 8/374 below 80; exact P=0.073 across three age groups). T was also absent among frail participants, which is the opposite of what a harmful allele would predict, and the frailty association was null (P=0.36). Treat this as an unconfirmed hint, not an individual lifespan or frailty estimate.

T/T at SIRT6 rs117385980 was not observed in either study (0 of 227 Iranian and 0 of 198 Finnish participants), which is expected for an allele with 0.5-3.5% frequency. The risk label only extends the non-significant direction seen in C/T carriers under an additive assumption; there are no data for this genotype, and it is not an individual lifespan or frailty estimate.
